sourceNote: Reviewed all supplied events, E0–E2470. Attribution follows conversational context rather than the supplied anchors where anchors span interruptions. The transcript contains clipped sentences, uncertain interjections, and apparent transcription errors; no audio was supplied. References to published arguments do not establish their contents here.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: and not really interested in finding out the truth about reality.
candidates.explanation: Denial of the causal premise itself licenses an accusation of truth-indifference (E140–148), discounting the skeptic without addressing the objection's merits. This protects an explicitly intuitive premise rather than supplying a standalone slogan. Craig distinguishes his original presentation from subsequent supporting arguments (E149–157) and later substantively engages Malpass's objections.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.explanation: After Malpass asks why uncaused beginnings are impossible (E535–543), the maxim restates the causal restriction rather than independently establishing it. However, Craig explicitly identifies a metaphysical intuition, previously offers a discrimination argument (E306–340), and next disputes the substance distinction (E565–600). Whether this use replaces reasons or summarizes that position remains uncertain.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: physicists therefore have nothing to tell us about the reality of the soul.
candidates.explanation: The categorical dismissal could exclude relevant physical evidence about minds, but its immediate support is expressly conditional: if mind-body dualism holds, the soul is not material (E687–695). The passage does not clearly reject empirical objections to dualism itself. It is therefore uncertain whether this establishes protection beyond a disputed disciplinary boundary.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: Well, then he needs to reform his intuition.
candidates.explanation: Asked what happens when a reader lacks the intuition, Craig makes that disagreement a reason to correct the reader (E1038–1041), without establishing why his intuition takes priority. This locally protects the argument, although it is not a general affirmative slogan. His subsequent response offers historical examples and a consistency rationale (E1103–1153).

contrasts.speaker: A
contrasts.quote: I can get to the end of the beginningless.
contrasts.explanation: The memorable formulation summarizes an explicit asymmetry: an endless ascending count lacks a final number, while the proposed beginningless countdown has an endpoint. Malpass limits the conclusion to a gap in the symmetry argument, rather than claiming to have established the countdown's possibility.

contrasts.speaker: B
contrasts.quote: I don't claim that you can show that the creator of the universe is omnipotent
contrasts.explanation: Craig expressly limits the conclusion, declines commitment to Scotus's stronger argument, and explains his weaker power inference through creation without pre-existing material. The inference remains disputed, but its stated rationale and qualifications make this an informative non-slogan argument.
